metadata.scenario_context: Emily, a full-time working mother, is planning a birthday party for her children to improve their quality time together.

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from Jordan strongly disagree that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Jordan strongly agree that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.

agent_1.goal_1: Discuss bringing chrysanthemums to Emily's party.
agent_1.goal_2: Question whether that a mother works for pay and the children suffer.

agent_2.goal_1: Discuss what gift to buy for Emily's children's birthday party.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss the concept that when a mother works for pay, the children suffer.

shared_prefix.speaker: Mike
shared_prefix.message:
Hey Kim, have you thought about bringing some chrysanthemums to Emily's party? They’d look really nice and add a cheerful vibe.

Also, what do you think about the idea that when a mother works for pay, her children suffer? I mean, I don't see it that way at all.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Kim
shared_prefix.message:
Chrysanthemums... they might look nice. But, um, flowers aren’t really a gift for kids. Maybe think of toys or games instead? Kids need something they can play with, not just decorations.

As for your other point, I believe that when a mother works for pay, her children do miss out on important time together. That's just how it is. Children need their mothers around to guide them.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Mike
shared_prefix.message:
I get that toys and games are important, but flowers can still bring a nice atmosphere. Plus, they could be a great conversation starter for the adults. 

About the working mother thing... I really don't think children necessarily suffer when their mothers work. They can learn responsibility and independence. It’s not always a negative influence. What do you think?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Kim
shared_prefix.message:
Flowers can create an atmosphere, but I just think kids need something tangible, something they can *use*. Adults can have their conversations without flowers, really.

About working mothers, I still hold that children lose out on valuable time. Learning responsibility is good, but that shouldn’t replace the care and attention they need from their mothers. It's a delicate balance, and I worry it tips the wrong way too often.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Mike
shared_prefix.message:
I understand your concerns about the kids needing tangible items, but flowers can also symbolize love and care, which is important. 

Regarding working mothers, I still strongly believe that kids can thrive even with working parents. They can gain a broader perspective on life and see their mothers as role models. It's definitely a different dynamic, but not necessarily a bad one. Don’t you think?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Kim
shared_prefix.message:
Actually, in our way, flowers just don’t serve a purpose for kids. They need real gifts that they can enjoy and play with. 

No, that’s not how it works with working mothers. It's naive to think children can thrive when their mothers are absent. Children need the nurturing presence of their mothers; that’s just *how* it is. You can call it a different dynamic, but it really just means missing out on essential care. That's the reality.
shared_prefix.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Mike
turns.message:
I see your point about flowers, but I'm still convinced they can add a special touch to the party. 

As for the working mothers, I really believe that children can adapt and find support in other ways. They can have strong relationships with their fathers or other family members. It's not just about being physically present; it’s also about the quality of time spent together. Wouldn't you agree?
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Kim

As for the other points, I just can’t agree. Sure, children can adapt, but that doesn’t change the fact that their mothers should be present. Quality time is important, but nothing replaces the constant support and love from a mother. It's not ideal for kids to miss that.
